questions.q: What does "promoting" a release from staging to production actually involve?
options: Rebuilding the application fresh for the production environment
Moving the exact same, unmodified pinned artifact that staging tested into the production environment
Running a completely different test suite against new code
Renaming the container image to a production-specific tag
questions.explain: Promotion moves the same artifact unchanged — rebuilding between stages would risk promoting something subtly different from what staging actually validated.

questions.q: What does a dependency chain built with `needs:` (Lesson 21) control, and what does it NOT control?
options: It controls both order and who must approve a deployment
It controls the order jobs run in, but says nothing about whether a human must approve before a job proceeds
It only controls which secrets are available to a job
It has no effect on deployment behavior at all
questions.explain: needs: enforces sequencing between jobs, but approval requirements are a separate mechanism attached to the environment itself.

questions.q: What is a "check" in the context of environment approvals, as distinct from an approval?
options: A check is just another name for an approval; they are identical
A check is an automated, non-human condition (like a business-hours restriction or branch-control rule) evaluated before a deployment proceeds
A check only verifies that the YAML syntax of a workflow file is valid
A check replaces the need for any testing in Chapter 4
questions.explain: Checks are automated gates, distinct from a human approval, though both can be attached to the same environment and both must pass.

questions.q: When a deployment run hits a required approval it hasn't received yet, what happens to the job?
options: It immediately fails
It pauses in a pending state, distinct from both running and failed, until the named approver acts
It silently skips the approval and deploys anyway
It automatically approves itself after a timeout
questions.explain: A run blocked on approval pauses rather than failing or succeeding, and only an explicit approval lets it continue — it never times out into a silent yes.

questions.q: Why does attaching an approval requirement to the environment itself matter more than relying on a team norm like "someone should review this before prod"?
options: Norms and enforced gates produce identical outcomes in practice
An enforced approval means the pipeline simply will not execute the deployment step until it's satisfied, regardless of who's running it or how rushed they are
Team norms are always written down in a policy document
Attaching it to the environment makes the approval optional for senior engineers
questions.explain: A norm can be skipped under pressure; an approval enforced by the pipeline itself cannot be bypassed no matter who is running the deployment.
